At the time, Mozambican democracy was only eight years old, and the government needed to present itself as a genuine democracy, transparent enough to attract foreign investment and distance itself from its authoritarian past. The trial was broadcast live on state television and radio. The then minister of justice 

explained

 the rationale, stating, “this is to show the country that there is transparency here, and that we are serious. . . .  people don’t trust the government, but this trial and the way it is being held publicly will help to end that.”

For similar reasons, the trial in the 

“Hidden Debts”

 case (

dívidas ocultas

) was broadcast live in 2021 and 2022. The case involved 19 defendants and $2 billion in loans granted in 2013 and 2014 by European and Russian banks. These loans were granted in secrecy without parliamentary approval. Both of these cases involved highly sensitive political information; nevertheless, they were broadcast. These precedents demonstrate that broadcasting a politically sensitive trial is not inherently incompatible with the administration of justice. Additionally, they illustrate that the decision to deny transmission requires more substantiation than an abstract appeal to judicial discretion.

The use of social media as a tool of political participation and mobilization is central to this discussion. During the protests, Mondlane developed a strategy that leveraged the generativity of the digital public. His livestreams were conducted on Facebook to tens of thousands of users, peaking on October 25, when he reached 115,000 concurrent viewers. The final report of the European Union Election Observation Mission documents that the very next day there was a 

national internet shutdown

.

Understood within the context of Mondlane’s political strategy, the court’s decision strips him of his principal vehicle of messaging. This may serve as yet another warning for political movements that have leveraged the digital public. Though the internet and social media may promise a safer, more democratic public within which people may strategize, organize, and mobilize, access to the internet is very much dispensed at the discretion of the state and corporations and can be suspended at their whims. The 

Zimbabwean

 and 

Kenyan

 protests of 2019 and 2024, respectively, provide examples of how easily states are able to react to social movements and collapse communications infrastructure. The point is not to foreclose the generative potential of social media but rather to illustrate how the control of digital infrastructure and platforms is central to guaranteeing this potential.

To be or not to be

The fact that this trial is taking place at all demonstrates the “stealth authoritarianism” of the Mozambican state. The legal scholar Melissa Crouch, building on Ozan Varol, 

uses the phrase

 to describe the manner in which an ostensibly democratic system can be wielded by the dominant political formation as a means of maintaining its power. Such a stealthily authoritarian state is furnished with a plethora of ideological and repressive apparatuses with which to quash opposition. The law is one such mechanism, available, at all times, to further authoritarian ends. It can palatably achieve results which could otherwise only be achieved through murders and kidnappings.

Apartheid-era South Africa was not a “stealth authoritarian” state, but a comparison is worth making. In 1968, the Department of Foreign Affairs proclaimed that “[t]he South African legal system is soundly based on the rule of law”; seven years later, the minister of justice, Jimmy Kruger, boasted in parliament that the country’s legal system was “held in high esteem in all Western countries,” as Alfred 

Cockrell records

. The point is not that the contemporary Mozambican state is equivalent to apartheid South Africa. Rather, the comparison illustrates how legal procedures and discourse can be deployed to legitimize a state that is obviously illegitimate. When the sheen of democracy and the rule of law is draped over a state, it becomes easy for those who are so inclined to pretend that what’s gilded is solid gold.

The 

2026 Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI) Country Report

 classifies Mozambique as a “clientelist state” presenting “the facade of electoral democracy.” This facade is an integral part of the resilience of authoritarian states. As a state constructed around and catered toward the interests of international, multinational, and multilateral clients, it is crucial that the state present itself as a palatable business partner. The concern is not with the actual operation of the state but rather with how it appears to operate. One is reminded of the famous joke told by Soviet workers: “We pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us.”

The seismic shock of the protests has shifted the landscape and disrupted the status quo of Mozambican politics. The government now finds itself in a double bind. On the one hand, the state cannot simply allow the opposition to organize itself and disseminate information as it very well pleases; this would spell the death of the liberation party’s 50-year rule. On the other hand, the government cannot resort to its tried and tested methods again in 2029, not only because the international client community is watching but, more importantly, because the chaos and destruction that may ensue could create an even more volatile situation.

The Mozambican state stands in the wake of a mass protest movement that presented the most politically legible threat to the liberation party since independence. Thus, it must be pragmatic in considering how best to secure its power. At this juncture, it appears that the safest choice is to rely on the judicial process to eliminate its most formidable threat from the political stage. While Mondlane will most likely not be jailed, he may be convicted, and in any case, the mere fact of this trial spells a transition in the state’s handling of political opposition. Moreover, the decision not to broadcast the trial seems to form part of this strategy, raising questions about the role of the digital public in the future of Mozambican political participation. 

The truth of the matter is that the merits of the state’s case are not of great importance; it would be naive to imagine that they are. Rather, the importance lies in the state’s quest for new methods of guaranteeing its resilience. If you will indulge the hyperbole, it is an existential quest: to be or not to be.

author: Azeezah Adekanmbi
title: Beyond survival
content:
Queer festivals are few and far between in West Africa. Those that afford the display of different media are even harder to come by. So, it was refreshing to see 

Obodo

 open its doors to people from across the continent for the 

Friends and Neighbours Festival

 in early October.

Participants gather at the Friends and Neighbours Festival in Lagos. Photo: © Daniella Almona.

The festival included workshops on fiction writing, poetry, arts and crafts, photography, film screenings, panel discussions, performance arts, drag shows and different forms of existing as a queer person. It brought, or rather returned, to the fore the versatility of the queer mind, the ability to fashion beauty even in the direst situations, and the hope to keep the light shining when survival feels like a threat.

Queerness has been regarded as an export of the West, and there has been little to no acknowledgement of queer Africans from precolonial times. What does it mean to define queerness in our own language and words outside Western thought? What does it mean to stop seeking permission?

Conversations focused on community building as an act of rebellion. Panel discussions featuring queer activists from different parts of Africa discussed the challenges of inter-border relations, conflicts foisted on queer Africans by imperial influence, and the roles our elected rulers play in tightening the noo

author: OAG
title: Picturing the bandits
content:
In June, the 

Guardian

 published 

“Brutal and Emboldened: How Nigeria’s Bandit Crisis Spun Out of Control,”

 a report from Katsina State in Nigeria’s northwest, where communities in local government areas such as Batsari have struck peace deals with the armed groups that have terrorized them for years. The photographs were taken by Terna Iwar, an Abuja-based photographer and artist who traveled with the 

Guardian

’s West Africa correspondent, Eromo Egbejule, and a local stringer — without a security escort — to meet one of those groups under a neem tree near the border with Niger.

On the latest episode of the 

Africa Is a Country

 podcast, the Nigerian Scam talks to Terna about that encounter: why he kept his camera in plain sight from the moment he arrived, how the group saw itself (as protectors of their communities, not bandits or terrorists), and what the peace deal actually gives them. Access to shops and medicine, and an end to their families’ shame, are on the table; disarmament is not, since other armed groups are still out there. Terna describes a landscape of abandoned towns and clinics, electricity poles without cables, and border posts that barely function. He also reflects on the central dilemma of conflict photography: how to portray people as more than one-dimensional without losing sight of the horrific acts they have committed.

Listen to the show below, and 

subscribe

 on your favorite platform.

Sa’eed Husaini

Well, look, I guess we should talk banditry and photography, which are some of the key words for the day. So yeah, we’re talking about banditry and shooting the bandits, quote, unquote, today. And the conversation is with a longtime comrade, collaborator, or friend, Terna Iwar, who’s also a well-known photographer, artist, and creative. So, Terna, thanks for coming on the show, man.

Terna Iwar

Thank you for having me.

Sa’eed Husaini

Homecoming in some ways, right?

Terna Iwar

In many ways, yes.

Sa’eed Husaini

We hope. So feel free to raid the fridge. You don’t need to take your shoes off. The normal protocol. So, this is inspired by a recent article, 

“Brutal and Emboldened,”

 a 

Guardian

 article about how Nigeria’s bandit crisis is spinning out of control. We want to talk about banditry, but not necessarily only about the dynamics and history and stuff. We’ve had part of that conversation previously with James Barnett, and we’ll have more of that kind of more historical, if you will, conversation going forward. But I think part of what we want to dive into is a bit of the experience, right, of encountering this camp, going to the camp, and shooting, or photographing, the bandits — and then, of course, your assessment, based on that experience, of what the hell is going on with banditry in Nigeria. I’m sure there’ll be elements of the conversation maybe you don’t want to get into right now. We’ll respect that, but of course, as detailed or as granular as you want to get, there’s space for that. And so, just by way of a little bit more background, Terna was part of a team that went up to Katsina, if I’m not mistaken, and had an exclusive interview with at least one camp of AK-47-wielding bandits. Got their perspective, but also kind of hung out with them. They seem pretty relaxed in the photos, and I guess it’d be interesting to get your take on how you got them to be so chilled out in the photos, and what they thought of you as well, shooting at them from the camera. So I don’t know, man. Maybe by way of intro, you could just talk a little bit about how you got into this and what that was about, and how freaked out were your parents hearing that you. . . .  However you want to get into it.

Terna Iwar

Well, again, thank you for having me. Talking about the work I do is not something I often get to do, so I think this might even help me metabolize what that was like. So Eromo, the West Africa correspondent for the 

Guardian

, reached out. We’d been talking back and forth for a while about potential stories and stuff that I was working on, what I was interested in doing, and when this came up, he thought that it would be a great fit, since a lot of the work that I’ve been doing in photojournalism revolves somehow around conflict. I just kind of found myself shooting a lot of conflict stuff, banditry, the aftermath of people’s lives changing in the most horrific, drastic ways. Initially, because of the nature of the story, it was very, very tightly kept. I didn’t even know specifically where we were going, but I knew the situation in Katsina, where I think 23 different local governments all have very intense bandit problems.

Sa’eed Husaini

Yeah, that’s insane.

Terna Iwar

And I had heard that there were efforts to curb that locally, not on a state or national level. And then in having conversations with Eromo, he let me know that there are groups of bandits that have accepted a peace deal with the local communities, for varying reasons. They chose to accept a peace deal. And so the goal was to go there, speak to the bandits, speak to the people that negotiated, speak to the communities, try and understand: What is this peace deal? Why would these bandits accept a peace deal? And why are they in banditry to begin with? Going there, we had a stringer, a contact on the ground, that helped us navigate. Of course, there were talks of, should we go with security? Should we not? Ultimately, we decided not to, because we felt very strongly at the time that showing up to these places with police or military would clamp down on the story and would basically make everyone unwilling to speak. And so we went there.

Sa’eed Husaini

I mean, probably it would have slightly increased the shootout possibility, right? I don’t know if you guys were thinking that, but it would seem to me.

Terna Iwar

Maybe if they were active bandits, then for sure. They would probably feel like we’re entrapping them or something, or it was a sting operation. But they had already accepted a peace deal. Reaching them was a whole different thing. We went to a community outside of the mining town, Nahuta, I believe before getting to Batsari, and we had to take a bike. I think it was like a 40-minute bike ride out of town to get to the mining town, and then another 15 minutes to get to where they were, because part of the deal was that they are not allowed to be in town within specific times, and I think they are not allowed to come into town with their weapons. Basically, their movement within the mining town and any town is very restricted, just so that everybody feels comfortable. And so we had to go out to them. Initially, I think they even wanted us to meet them at their base camp, but we eventually negotiated a neutral place, under a neem tree, to meet them.

Sa’eed Husaini

Yeah, that’s nuts. So you did meet them, and — could you just talk us through, before we get to the meeting itself and what the vibe was like there, what were you thinking that morning, when you guys were going to head out to go meet up with bandits? Was there any part of you that was thinking, 

Damn, this could be it

? Or were you feeling pretty confident about the peace deal? Were you like, N

o, it’s fine, the peace deal will keep things safe

?

Terna Iwar

Well, I think a thing about it, for me specifically — I can’t speak for anyone else — is if you’ve done your due diligence, you can only work based on the information that you have. And the information I had was these people were willing to talk. They had accepted the peace deal. That was the information I had. And not to say journalists are never betrayed, or that the people who are willing to talk to you might not turn on you, but from everything I had read and researched, it wasn’t a very common occurrence. And it seemed to me like a lot of these groups do want to tell their story. They have a need to be out there just as much, or to be seen as people rather than boogeymen. I think every terror group out there, at least in this day and age, is trying to sanitize itself in one way or the other. And plus, if you’re going to do this type of work, you can’t think of the worst-case scenario. You take it into consideration. You list all the things that could go wrong, and then you work to minimize your risk. We did do a very thorough risk assessment before we went there.

Sa’eed Husaini

No, fair enough. At one level, it sort of sounds like a more intense version of living in Nigeria, doesn’t it?

Terna Iwar

That is exactly right. That is exactly right.

Sa’eed Husaini

It’s not like anybody’s guaranteed anything, really. No, that’s a fair point. When you talk about them wanting their story to be told — of course, there’ve been a few investigations that have talked to them directly. There was, of course, the BBC documentary. Different group — I think that was a Zamfara group, right? And now Katsina. And James Barnett and Murtala Ahmed Rufa’i and various people have been talking to them. We interviewed James Barnett a while back. But this is as close as we’ve gotten, in a way — having someone who’s within our ranks very much face to face with the bandits. And it’s that face-to-face element I want to now explore. I suspect OAG wants to come in with questions. But so you arrive at the neem tree, and it’s a bunch of guys. Some of them have dreads, the kind of military uniforms in some cases. What was your first impression seeing the guys, and how did you folks feel received? And sorry, how did you feel about the camera? Did that require extensive negotiation?

Terna Iwar

Well, not even. Whenever I go to any place where it’s fairly dangerous — well, depending on the kind of danger — I don’t want to hide. In this particular case, I wanted them to see the camera and be comfortable with the fact that there is a camera on the scene right from the jump. So I didn’t put it in my bag. It was right in front of me, facing everyone, from even before we got to Batsari. And then when we got to Batsari, because we had to wait a little bit, I was already taking pictures, I was already making images, walking around, familiarizing myself, and in a very large way, familiarizing anyone that would come up to us with the camera. If I had gotten there, and then after they start talking, I suddenly whip out a camera, I’m sure they would be like, W

ait, wait, wait, what’s happening here

? But right from arrival, the camera was very visible. And then I asked them directly — or, well, asked — but basically I raised it up, and I was like, “I’m here, notice me,” and I immediately started taking pictures. So I think there is a little bit of audacity, but also you kind of have to sensitize people to the camera. Even if it wasn’t bandits, if it was anyone, a camera suddenly being put in your face is not nice. It’s actually quite aggressive.

Sa’eed Husaini

That sounds like experience talking, because now that you say it, it makes perfect sense. But one might have been tempted to be a bit shy with it, or, as you say, pull it out of your bag mid-conversation. But I can see how that would be maybe a terrible idea. So now I’m really curious about — no, let me let you keep going. I thought you were going to say something.

Terna Iwar

I was going to say that it is a good point about being shy, because I’m not generally the very forward, aggressive type. So I think maybe some of the ways in which I interact with these guys are very careful, even as I’m trying to capture stuff that can be dangerous.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. And so I’m curious about what their impressions of you guys were, and whether they made jokes, or how they read you guys in this.

Terna Iwar

I would give a lot of credit to the stringer. I think he did a lot of work to familiarize himself with them, or to get in their good books, because when we got there, they were very prepared to have a conversation. I would even imagine that they went out of their way — not that I know what they do all day, but I would imagine that they moved things around to make it happen. Before we got there, we were told that we should bring Coke, Fanta, and bread, because it’s apparently a very strong sign, and a thing that a lot of these bandit groups love. We didn’t, but we were told that that would help in the appeasement. But when we got there, they were relatively welcoming. Of course, there were some people that were very standoffish. There were some people that were giving us not very good looks. But in the main, they were very welcoming. I think even later on, at some point, they offered us Coke and food, when they were going on break and for prayers.

Sa’eed Husaini

That’s interesting, and again, it doesn’t necessarily align with the portrayal that one generally gets from a distance about what these guys are like. Even the talk about Coke and bread — in the civil society kind of reports, there’s a lot of emphasis laid on drugs and people being kind of out of their minds and being a bit reckless, but the guys you’re describing don’t sound exactly like that. So what were your first impressions, really? From the pictures, clearly the guys were armed. But beyond those basic facts, did they appear and give off a vibe that you expected? Did anything stand out?

Terna Iwar

In many ways, yes. I would say I’ve been to a prison or two before, and I’ve shot many different places that were going through very tough times, and what I found is most people in most places are not that different. The circumstances and the things they do might be different. Look, what I’ll say is, in all my time on this earth, I’ve met maybe two people who I looked into their eyes and I knew this person had killed a person. I just knew. But most people don’t wear either their atrocities or their traumas on their sleeve. They find ways to bury all of that very deeply. And when you meet them, you don’t know what someone is or what they’ve done. It was no different with these guys. They just seemed like regular people, until you started talking to them about what they are doing. Because ultimately they are still bandits, peace deal or no peace deal. It’s not until you get into the details, into the weeds, that you realize, okay, this person — we don’t see the world the same way. But first impressions are always like, yeah, regular guy.

OAG

A guy you could play football with.

Terna Iwar

Yeah, you could literally. And they start telling you about their own hopes and dreams, and you’re like, okay, regular guy. But then, if you talk about the other stuff, their banditry and their way of life and all that, it’s very horrific. So in some ways I wasn’t surprised. I was a little bit surprised by their unwillingness to engage with what they were doing, but people always make excuses and rationalize all kinds of things.

OAG

It’s interesting, what you’re saying about them not engaging with what they are doing, and the general perception of what people think. But let’s step back and zoom in on them. Do they keep tabs on the political scenery — the bandits, I’m saying, who we are assuming have some sort of amnesty going on? Are they interested in Peter Obi, or are they Obidient? Would they like for Kwankwaso to be there? That type of thing. And do they maybe think they’re going to graft into the political thing, like voting? If they’re not going to do that, then is it going to be by way of arms? Because people that are looking to have their sins forgiven and maybe at some time be reintegrated back into society — do they see themselves. . . .  Maybe the broader question I’m asking is: Do they see themselves participating politically, voting, then at some point integrating back into society and being normal, in quotes? Their hopes and aspirations of being normal, and not staying in the bush forever. Did you get a sense of that from the discussion?

Terna Iwar

Yes, there is an awareness. Actually, I would say there is a very strong awareness of social injustice — social injustice in that they and their people have been disenfranchised by the government. That was a thing that they kept coming back to when we were discussing why they are doing what they are doing. There was a very strong emphasis from them that the government has failed them. That was part of why they said they were doing what they are doing, and part of why they kept doing it, because they said successive governments would make promises and would never keep them. There was even a little bit of lamentation there, where they were like, they’ve tried to talk to the government, and there are a lot of people that don’t want to engage. Now, I should say, there are, I think, over 30 different bandit groups. We were told that there were many, many bandit groups, some operating across different communities. Some have basically made a community their home base. And so nothing that these guys say speaks for all these bandit groups, but for these guys specifically, this is what they were talking about. They had tried to talk to the government. They’d tried negotiating with the government even before they became bandits. It was because the government was not fulfilling their end of the deal. They talk about how they took up arms to begin with to try and protect their people, ostensibly from other bandit groups.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. So they were vigilantes in some way, previously.

Terna Iwar

They much prefer that term, 

vigilante

, to 

bandits

. Because the leader of the group, Abu Radde, said he really didn’t like the term 

bandits

 or 

terrorists

. It makes them upset. They are not criminals.

OAG

What would he have preferred?

Terna Iwar

Well, they feel like they are doing all of this to protect their people.

Sa’eed Husaini

Yeah. So the vigilante or community security kind of thing.

Terna Iwar

They didn’t use the term 

vigilante

, but they did say they are doing it to protect their people.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. Pretty crazy. No, OAG, let me let you in.

OAG

Yeah, but in the face of insecurity, do they have an idea of how they’ve been branded, and how the federal government, or maybe even the state government, is working to kind of flush them out? Do they understand the kind of negative PR they are getting?

Terna Iwar

They understand that very clearly. Yes.

OAG

So that’s my point. If they are seeing it this way, and the bloodshed component of their work is becoming more pronounced these days — I know they said they’ve tried to talk to the government — have they explored maybe other ways? I know it’s just political, but maybe forming a political pressure group or something, without the violent aspect. That’s why I was asking more about their politics.

Sa’eed Husaini

You’re trying to push your own solution, right? They need to register with INEC.

Terna Iwar

No, I don’t think they are thinking in terms of political solutions at all. They are done with that. I think they’ve done what they’ve seen other communities do, and what they know how to do. It seems like the logical conclusion, or the logical next step, for them is to take up arms, not explore politics or go into politics or try and change things through the system.

OAG

So did they come up with any form of suggestions that would make them consider dropping their arms, or anything that they want the government to do for them to then consider dropping their arms? Did they mention anything?

Terna Iwar

Well, I think that is included in the peace deal. The peace deal does not include disarmament. They find themselves in a situation where all of them have families. They have parents who are part of communities that I believe they’ve also terrorized. So their families are now pariahs, or were pariahs, and part of what they wanted was for their families to be able to move around without feeling shame. One. And for they themselves to gain access to, well, the amenities of civilization: be able to go to the shop and buy something, buy biscuits, be able to get medication — just the benefits that you get from living as part of a community with some sort of economy. And in exchange, they agreed not to terrorize anyone. They refused to give up their guns, because they said there are other groups that are still — because remember that they are still herders, specifically. They are still herders, and I believe — well, maybe not them, I don’t know — but they are protecting their cattle from rustlers and other bandit groups. So they said that they can’t give up their weapons because these other groups are not giving up their weapons, and they need to protect themselves. But it comes back to — that’s why they couldn’t come into town, because they can’t come into town with their weapons.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. All this talk about the government — their views on the government — sort of inspires a certain question. Because all this time, actually, we’ve said very little about the security agencies. You mentioned you considered the pros and cons of having some of them around, but looking at the images you shared, it doesn’t really look like there’s much security presence. And even in the story you’re telling, of them feeling the need to stay armed because there are other armed groups, nowhere are they mentioning going to report to the police. As somebody living in Nigeria, we can all imagine why that’s the case. But I just wonder, going out there, how remote or ungoverned, quote, unquote, do these spaces appear? Was there any government presence at all? Did you see schools out there, or electricity? Or are they really just kind of out there, cut off from the governed bits of Nigeria?

Terna Iwar

To a large extent, I think the 

Guardian

 did a fantastic — well, it is part of the body of work that we’re doing, but they put out an article talking about the insecurity across the Sahel, and a thing that they found is that the Sahel and these northern parts of Nigeria are places that the government doesn’t really penetrate into. I think either th ey find it difficult to govern, or there are not enough resources, natural resources, there for them to really care about. Or, for whatever reason, there is very little presence of the government or any governing structures there.I didn’t see a school. But again, we stopped off in town — we took a car, stopped off in the township, and then took a bike, almost 40 minutes, 30, 40 minutes’ bike ride into the wilderness, really. And we passed through several abandoned towns. We even passed through an aid center — it used to be a hospital, or a clinic, sorry — that was abandoned when bandits had destroyed it. We passed abandoned towns, abandoned clinics. On our way there, we saw signs of burgeoning development, in that there were electricity poles that had been placed to take light to certain remote areas, but there were no cables on them. So I guess maybe that project was also abandoned. This area that we’re in, I would say, is really just abandoned. The government is not — or maybe they tried at some point in time, but they are not trying to connect these areas to the rest of the country. And where we actually met them was even more remote. Just bare fields and trees for miles around.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. Okay.

Terna Iwar

And plus, where we were is very close to the border. In fact, before we went to meet them, we did go to three different border points with Niger. There’s not very much there either.

Sa’eed Husaini

Even the people who live there?

Terna Iwar

Yeah, people live there, but yeah.

Sa’eed Husaini

So would you know it’s a border, or is it that people just say, “Hey, this is a border”?

Terna Iwar

No, we went to the known ones. The main one — as I understand it, not a lot of people use it, but it’s very official. The road is done, the gate is very big, there is security there. They check whatever they are checking. They inspect cars and all that. Very built-out situation. The second border crossing we saw was basically three security guys and a hut with a plank across. The third one had a customs office, and this was the one that is close to Batsari — well, closer, a couple of miles away from Batsari. They had the customs building there, but as far as I’m aware, it’s not operational. Perhaps it is. I don’t know. But it didn’t seem like it was operational.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. And how you’re describing it, it also didn’t seem like if you rode through with 100 guys on motorcycles and AKs, anything would really stop you. You could probably just keep going.

Terna Iwar

Plus, how do you police miles and miles of — you could drive a kilometer on either side of any one of these borders, cross, and no one could stop you. It’s not like there’s a long fence. Well, it’s only America that can do such a thing.

Sa’eed Husaini

And even there.

Terna Iwar

And even there, you could drive on either side of the border and just cross. Which is literally what these guys do.

Sa’eed Husaini

I mean, who can blame them? Borders, of course, classically an administrative fiction more than anything. Really fascinating. I know we’ve kept you for a while. Just another couple of questions before we let you go. I want to come back to seeing this through the lens of a photographer, but one more detail that stuck in my mind is this mining question. Because you stopped by a mining town, and for a lot of Nigerians, one easy explanation of banditry — even for some kinds of left analysts, or at least let’s call them anti-imperialist analysts — has been that this is all about mining: that there are foreign interests in cahoots with certain domestic interests that control the mines, and the bandits are just a distraction, or they’re just the security guys that make sure that the illicit mining global conglomerates or cabals continue to extract their coins from these areas. Not to force you to respond to all of that, but how did the mining element seem connected, if at all, to the lives of these guys? Do these guys mine, or do they go around the mines? Or did it feel like two different dynamics altogether?

Terna Iwar

The guys at the mines were very clear, and they were very insistent, that the bandits, Abu Radde’s group, have nothing to do with their operations.

Sa’eed Husaini

Interesting.

Terna Iwar

Yeah, they were very insistent that that was the case. I can’t say anything to that, because to my mind, I don’t see how that could be. But they insisted that that’s the case — that they don’t interfere, and they’ve never interfered, and they don’t pay a tax to the bandits.

OAG

Let me just jump in. Is there a general message that they have? Because with social media and all, we see it — and it might not be the same ones you’re talking about — but we see them flaunting money, even doing giveaways and all that. And I think popularity and fame is starting to creep in with bandits now. So do they have a general message which they’re trying to pass across? And what would their vision of the future be like? Because I’m sure they don’t want to be bandits — well, I don’t want to say I’m sure they don’t want to be bandits forever — but what would their picture of the future be like, coming from your interaction with them and the feelers that you got from them?

Terna Iwar

From them, I didn’t get very. . . .  I mean, Abu Radde himself was very excited to be going on Hajj. This is one of the things that he was very excited about now that there is a peace deal. There was another young guy — I think he’s like 17, even — who had left school to join Abu Radde’s gang, and he seemed excited to go back. Well, if not excited, he was very interested in the idea of going back to school. He left in SS1 or so. So a lot of the guys that we spoke to — these are the kinds of things that they cared about in their future.

Sa’eed Husaini

It almost seems like banditry is kind of a part-time thing, or a transitional thing, for a lot of people. They’re doing it, but it’s not the only thing they do, or the only thing they want to do. It’s just kind of part of their hustle. Not to be simplistic, but is that unfair?

Terna Iwar

I would say it is not unfair, in that my impression is, if they felt like they had other options, they wouldn’t be bandits.

Sa’eed Husaini

Got it.

Terna Iwar

But banditry is a thing where, once you step in, you’re already in. Like podcasting — you’re staying. You can’t be a bandit part-time, I don’t think so, and it doesn’t seem like they even are bandits part-time. But it is also true that they want more for themselves than being bandits. It seemed, again, from their perspective, from what they were saying, that this is not the life that they chose — or they chose that life because they had no choice. When we asked them, “Okay, so what about all the people that you’ve killed, all the destruction, death?,” their simple answer, which again was an avoidant thing, was, “Things happen.” Things happen. But they kept coming back again to the fact that they are only doing this because the government has failed them.

Emeka Ugwu

I joined late, and I’ve been listening for the most part, trying to get a sense of where the conversation is coming from and where it’s going. So my own question is maybe a spinoff from my failure to get a holistic grip of the conversation. But I’m interested, ideologically — and I don’t want to label it Islamic — in ideas about what awaits them in the afterlife. So my question is: Is there any sense that these guys don’t have a sex life? Do they have conversations about women? Are they getting married?

Terna Iwar

There are a lot of them that are married.

Emeka Ugwu

No mass marriage, all that?

Terna Iwar

Well, I don’t know. Abu Radde, I know, is married. I know a couple of the other guys are married. I don’t know about the young guys. We asked them what they do for fun, and they said that there’s this game that they play where they basically beat each other to impress women. I’m blanking on the word.

Sa’eed Husaini

I’ve seen this.

Terna Iwar

I think it’s a game of endurance, where they are whipping each other. I found that fascinating.

Emeka Ugwu

Isn’t that more of a cultural thing? Because right from when I was young, they’d say if you want to marry, in some parts of the north, you endure some kind of beating. I don’t know if that’s more cultural than anything else.

Terna Iwar

Yeah, I only bring that up because Emeka was asking about marriage. So clearly they’re — 

Sa’eed Husaini

Interested in babes. Some of them are married. As elsewhere in the world, there are cultural particularities around courtship. I’ve heard of 

Shadi

 before. I’ve seen some videos, too, of guys in the Sahel putting on what looks like makeup and dancing in a row — guys who dance the hardest.

Emeka Ugwu

Would that be a tribal thing, I would think? Would that be right?

Sa’eed Husaini

I mean, so this relates to maybe my penultimate question, which is around swag. They were dressed cleanly in the pictures you took.

Terna Iwar

They had brand-new bikes.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. The bikes were new. The military fatigues were sort of sharp. They looked kind of ironed, and they were also kind of posing. There was a guy who was rocking a mean-ass cigarette. They had gloves and stuff. The guys had dreads. Can you talk us through the swag a bit? Because I kind of felt like they were swagging out a little bit. Not to summarize it, but was there an element of coolness at play here?

Terna Iwar

I think the particular guy you’re thinking of, with the long dreads and the dark shades — I think that’s just him. He’s also the one that I mentioned was interested and a little bit excited about going back to school. So I don’t know about. . . . 

Sa’eed Husaini

Youthful exuberance.

Terna Iwar

Yeah, I think maybe he’s at that point in his life, and, being not far from, I guess, the wider culture, there are things that he’s interested in that maybe some of the other guys aren’t.

Sa’eed Husaini

Right. So he might have a TikTok account, maybe.

Terna Iwar

But there is a thing about uniforms, especially military uniforms. Despite the fear that they evoke in Nigeria, I think there’s a way in which uniforms have been designed to look sharp. It’s hard to see a person in fatigues that does not look a certain kind of imposing and sharp. I guess my question would be, how did they get access to it? I’m thinking about that now, and I don’t know why it didn’t occur to me then.

Sa’eed Husaini

As with a lot of vigilante or community protection kinds of groups, they seem to end up with one form of uniform or the other. In a way, these things are things you can buy in the market too. Even the army guys buy their own uniforms in the market.

Emeka Ugwu

Ah, so true. The same way army personnel buy their own.

So, staying on this swag thing. I’d imagine that bandits who are — I don’t even know whether to call them bandits — but young and have TikTok accounts, there would be some trend within the larger society. Of course, because of location, that would be hard. But when they raid, they make money. That’s why they flaunt it. Flaunt it for what? For who? What are they flaunting? Are they telling the Nigerian population that banditry pays? Or are they trying to use TikTok the way I think it’s used within that generation — some of them use it to show off, maybe to impress women? I think some of these social media platforms really promote stuff like hookup culture. Or is it that these guys are not even participants in this? I think some research has suggested that that’s why they go and kidnap schoolgirls. I’m not saying this particular group that you’ve spoken to, but I’d imagine they want to wear some of the trendiest sunshades, boots. Because at the end of the day, why is it a racket that pays, and why is it something that they are drawn to over time, to the point where they feel the urge to show off their loot — again, not this particular group, but even some bandits that rustle cows? Or I don’t know whether vigilantes are paid for any of the work that they do, at least up in that region. Because I’m almost certain that vigilantes in the southeast who look out for bandits, or who are trying to act as security against bandits — I don’t know how well they are paid, if they’re even paid. I’m sure they are not paid well.

Terna Iwar

I think there are a bunch of different types of these bandit groups. There are the ones that are very Islamist in what they’re doing — they’re pushing the religious agenda. And then there are other ones who are, I think, doing it for money. These guys, again, say that they’re doing it to protect their people and to protect themselves from other bandit groups.

Emeka Ugwu

And their cows.

Terna Iwar

And their cattle, yeah.

Sa’eed Husaini

In their own self-conception.

Terna Iwar

In their own mind, yeah. In their own self-conception, yes. But I think the broader thing here, to your question, Emeka, I think there is a culture in Nigeria of money above all, and it might be that these groups that are celebrating and boasting on social media are tapping into something that is a broader occurrence in Nigeria. It’s hard to be young on social media and not buy into the broader value system that is being promoted.

Sa’eed Husaini

My final question, and probably should be our final question, just because we’ve kept you for a while. It’s maybe a general question that you’ve encountered before, around conflict journalism and conflict photography, but I wonder how you think about it in this case. Talking to you now, I feel some sympathy for these guys, right? I think you’ve kind of humanized them, because they don’t really look like this sort of bloodthirsty — 

Terna Iwar

It’s not by intention.

Sa’eed Husaini

No, but if you explore anybody’s perspective enough, they come across as not just irrational and bloodthirsty — 

Terna Iwar

Not one-dimensional.

Sa’eed Husaini

That’s the main thing, really. They come across as not one-dimensional. They’re multidimensional suddenly. And of course, looking at the images you took of them, too, they’re respectful images, right? You’ve not treated them as clowns or African savages. In the pictures, they look human. They just look like people one might meet. I guess the question is an ethical one. You’ve also highlighted that these are people who have — in their own telling, and the groups that they affiliate with, or bandits more generally, as we all know — committed some pretty heinous atrocities. How does one strike the balance? As a photographer, how do you think about managing that tension between trying to portray people as people, meaning not one-dimensional, but then also grappling with the tragedy and the trauma that this whole phenomenon has brought about? I’m sure there’s no easy answer to that, but I just wonder what your thinking on that is.

Terna Iwar

That is one of the central questions for me, actually, because at every point in time, I’m very aware of who these guys are, or what they have done, right? I see my work — as passé or as bland as it may sound — as witnessing what is happening, carrying a story back so that everybody else can understand. I try very hard not to place judgment on whoever the subject is. I think a part of what I’m doing requires me to be able to understand the person in front of me in a way, but at the same time, not pass judgment. I don’t want my subjective perspective to taint or to paint or to color the work I’m doing. Inevitably, it’s hard to do that, and I guess even the fact that I’m trying to understand who I’m working with, the people that I’m taking pictures of, also comes out in the images. But really, ultimately, I’m there to witness and to tell the story as I’ve seen it. If I had gone there and the feeling of the place was very tense and violent, and you could smell the smoke in the air and see death in these people’s eyes, the images probably would have shown that. That wasn’t what I saw. But the thing that I worry about is this humanizing aspect, right? Because I do see them as more than one-dimensional. But at the same time, it’s important to hold several ideas in your head at the same time. These are human beings that have wants, needs, desires. They want more for themselves. They believe it is their right, and I can see how that is true for almost anyone. But at the same time, they committed horrible, irredeemable acts, and that also has to be front and center and reckoned with. And sometimes I worry that the work I’m making does not actually properly capture both sides. But in going there, I have a way in which I approach making images, and so far it’s worked. It allows people to open up. It definitely allowed them to feel a bit more comfortable with me, which I think is only a good thing.

Sa’eed Husaini

I agree. I think it’s credit to your skills and experience, and it’s helpful for observers, because it doesn’t do us any favors to try to simplify them or see them in a one-dimensional register. I think it is important to actually try to grapple with that tension, and not resolve it so easily either way, because that doesn’t lend itself to sustainable solutions either. So I think you’ve done very important work here — of course, you and the 

Guardian

 and Eromo.

Terna Iwar

Excellent work by Eromo. He’s amazing.

Sa’eed Husaini

Absolutely, and he’s somebody we’d be very keen to talk to as well. But not only because you’re our guy, but also because I think the photographer’s lens — a picture says a thousand words, for sure, but getting the context of how those pictures were taken, and why, and what the moment felt like, is also very enriching. So, look, thanks for making the time to have this conversation.

Terna Iwar

No, thank you for having me.

Sa’eed Husaini

Amazing. Hope we can have it again, maybe on a slightly lighter subject matter. Emeka, any final thoughts? Vote of thanks?

Emeka Ugwu

No, that’s it.

Sa’eed Husaini

Fair enough. Okay, Terna, nice one, man. We’ll let you go. Stay well.

Terna Iwar

Stay safe, folks. Cheers, guys.

Sa’eed Husaini

All right, man. Take care, fellas.

author: Branko Marcetic
title: The left can defeat reactionaries
content:
The United States left has been so conditioned in the Trump era to look aghast and horrified at election results that it is still hard to fully believe the outcome of the November 3 midterms. Yet those historic events really did happen: Donald Trump and Republicans suffered a historic rebuke from voters, handing Democrats wins up and down the ballot all across the country, flipping both chambers of Congress in their favor, and handing them the largest congressional majorities they’ve had since Barack Obama’s election.

In many ways, the result is simple. Across poll after poll leading into the election and exit poll after exit poll leading out of it, the message from voters was the same: they think the economy sucks, they think prices are too high, and they’re angry at Trump and blame him squarely for this entire situation. To send this message, voters turned out in droves to hand power to a Democratic Party that these same polls show they have very little love for, sometimes viewing the Dems even more dimly than they do Trump.

Democrats were expected to take the House. They were 

not expected

 to win a majority of more than 250 seats in it, as estimates at the time of writing had them winning. Nor were they expected to win a Senate majority, let alone a Senate majority of at least 54 seats. And they were not expected to flip deep red seats across the country, to sweep Republicans from control of Texas at nearly every level of power, and to win a 

majority of the country’s governorships

, achieving 

wins and trifectas

 in states they’ve been practically locked out of, sometimes for decades. Obama referred to his 2010 midterms rout as a “shellacking.” These midterms were an annihilation.

This is not just good news for Democrats. For the US left, which operates within these Democratic majorities at both the state and federal levels, the results present a historic opportunity to turn its political priorities from words into tangible reality across the country, further building the power it has patiently and, for a long time, quietly been constructing from the ground up these past 

10 years

.

That includes at the federal level. Even though Trump has two more years in the White House, and Democrats are threatening to zealously turn their powers of oversight on the vast record of abuse and criminality he’s racked up during that time, there is some, extremely slim reason to believe something could actually get done.

Trump 

phoned

 Politico on election night to make clear he was open to working with the Democrats and didn’t “want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” The last time Trump was in the White House with a Democratic-controlled House, during the pandemic, the United States saw the largest expansion of the welfare state in decades. Trump’s ideological malleability and the fact that he is currently looking at a legacy as a historic failure presents at least the possibility of an opening for something better to happen.

It’s an opening the left will be able to take advantage of, too. The left will enter this new Congress with far more formidable numbers than it’s had in decades: at least seven members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), creating the historic opportunity to form, for the first time, a distinct 

socialist caucus

 in Congress and a Squad-like progressive “

Bloc

” that could have as many as 20 members.

The massive Democratic House majority means “the Bloc” will not have the expected leverage of being able to block House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries’s bid for Speaker, or to hold up legislation Freedom Caucus–style. But it will have influence. Much of the generous pandemic policies of 2020, including both Trump and, later, Joe Biden’s stimulus checks, originated with the public demands of socialist and progressive members of Congress that later found their way into legislation on the back of their clear public need and popularity.

This time, the left will be making these arguments in a world in which socialists have already transformed the way even centrist Democrats talk about politics. The party’s years-long obsession with “norms” and rescuing democracy having largely faded into the background in favor of the affordability-focused and anti-billionaire rhetoric 

popularized

 by, respectively, New York’s socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the socialist duo of Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour.

Just as importantly, it’s a world in which the left, thanks to a spate of major wins on November 3, has thoroughly discredited the arguments used to marginalize and dismiss its basic case.

No left-wing victory of the night was bigger than Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan Senate win over Republican Mike Rogers by a whopping seven points. It was the exact, hefty margin El-Sayed himself had 

promised

 he would win by back in May and defied the incessant predictions that he would end up badly underperforming.

There was arguably no more important race this year than for the purple state’s Senate seat: for the US left, which sought to prove progressives could run and win outside of blue strongholds; for corporate Democrats, a segment of whom feared losing the ability to fearmonger about supposedly risky left-wing candidates; for the pro-Israel lobby, which feared that the success of a stridently pro-Palestinian message would obliterate its claim that blind fealty to Israel was “good politics”; for Trump and the MAGA movement, whose loss of the key state could be a harbinger of even worse political defeat to come.

El-Sayed’s win has confirmed all of these. It represents not just a failure for MAGA, in the form of now two-time loser and career-long warmonger Mike Rogers. It’s an absolute disaster for the pro-Israel lobby and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in particular, which blew tens of millions of dollars over the course of both the primary and general to defeat El-Sayed and tried every trick in the book to defame and make voters, particularly Jewish ones, fear him.

Instead, both 

exit polls

 and 

voting data

 indicate El-Sayed comfortably won Jewish voters despite this ugly, Islamophobic campaign against him. He outperformed Kamala Harris in the heavily Jewish Oakland County, the home base of his Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, who humiliated herself trying to kneecap him in the final days of the race.

Catastrophically for the pro-Israel lobby, he did all this while maintaining an unabashed opposition to further US aid to Israel, proving unambiguously that left-wing criticisms of Israeli policy are not only broadly shared by voters in battleground states, but that they are shared by Jewish voters, too.

That he managed this is especially impressive given that, unlike his Democratic colleague running for governor, El-Sayed had to overcome not only an 

avalanche

-on-election-eve-XsnwXX3fPTPpiTU18nRE) of big money spending but also members of his own party working around the clock to sabotage him, from Stevens’s last-minute endorsement of Rogers to Rep. Hillary Scholten’s 

support

 for a 

write-in campaign

 against the Democratic nominee in the final days.

Democratic defectors to the GOP had a variety of motives, but at least some of them made publicly clear they hoped El-Sayed’s defeat would nip the growing Democratic opposition to US aid to Israel in the bud — something they were willing to elect a candidate who included 

actual antisemites

 in his campaign to do, as well as to empower an administration that makes common cause with literal neo-Nazis and white supremacists. Instead, they lost and disgraced themselves for nothing.

El-Sayed also did it on a progressive platform of Medicare for All and taxing the rich, two ideas that, when Bernie Sanders first popularized them in 2016, the public was told were too controversial with swing voters and risky to run on. A decade later, these ideas have such widely understood, popular support that Republicans didn’t even bother attacking them. Instead, they put all their eggs in the race-baiting basket, making El-Sayed’s Arab ethnicity and Muslim faith the overwhelming focus of their attacks in what turned out to be one of the most shockingly racist election campaigns this century — and another disgraceful failure.

El-Sayed’s win wasn’t the only bright spot for the left on election night. There was also Troy Jackson’s win in Maine, who succeeded where four others had failed in unseating the seemingly untouchable 30-year Republican incumbent Susan Collins from her Senate seat. Though Jackson, an 18-year state legislator and former state senate president and Democratic leader, was far from your typical image of a left insurgent, he quickly consolidated socialist and progressive backing after former nominee Graham Platner’s personal scandals pushed him out of the race.

Though not a socialist, Jackson’s genuine working-class background — as a fifth-generation logger who 

entered politics

 to win collective bargaining rights for his fellow woodworkers — and robust progressive record made him closer to the kind of candidates the left hopes to see in power. In the end, Jackson was able to secure victory by neutralizing Collins’s ability to run up big scores in otherwise blue-voting areas.

The other major progressive win was by James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Texas seat in 38 years, part of a historic blue sweep across Texas that saw Democrats end nearly three decades of GOP rule of the state. Talarico is 

not a socialist

, despite 

old comments

 criticizing capitalism that briefly became a campaign issue, and like El-Sayed, he took pains to 

insist

 that he was a capitalist. Even so, he was backed by groups like 

More Perfect Union

 and the 

Progressive Change Campaign Committee

 and drew support from prominent socialists like 

Hasan Piker

, who has said that the left was “the force that backed him early on” and “allowed him to win.”

Maybe more important, Talarico ran on a 

class-based message

 decrying “

billionaire mega-donors

” — one of whom, Elon Musk, lit at least 

$47 million

 on fire trying and failing to beat him — and insisting that the fundamental political divide in the United States was “top versus bottom,” a more progressive message than many Democrats ran on even in solid blue states. So his emphatic 12-point victory over the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton is a victory for the kind of populist message the left has long advocated, even as Talarico did things like refusing to back Medicare for All and 

declining

 to campaign with Bernie Sanders when he visited the state.

Speaking of Sanders, as of the time of writing, 17 of the 21 candidates endorsed by the socialist senator have won their races, while only two have lost, and two are in races that are still to be called. Sanders’s endorsements were less straightforwardly left-wing than those of organizations like DSA or Justice Democrats. They included candidates like El-Sayed and Jackson, but they also included more establishment candidates like Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, who beat corporate-friendly rivals in their primaries. They ran the gamut from DSA candidates like New York’s 

Claire Valdez

 and Colorado’s 

Melat Kiros

 to candidates like Rebecca Cooke, the less progressive candidate in her primary but someone who 

flipped

 a Trump-voting, rural Wisconsin district that for decades was represented by a Democrat.

They also included William Lawrence, the Sunrise Movement cofounder who has flipped a swing district in the swing state of Michigan despite having one of the more left-wing résumés of any Democratic candidate — something that, like El-Sayed, we were told would make him a guaranteed loser. The fact that Lawrence left DSA mid-campaign and had to distance himself from 

old tweets

 that included calls to nationalize the fossil fuel industry should not take away from the magnitude of his win. On the back of a 

progressive populist

 campaign that pushed a 

data center moratorium

 and 

Medicare for All

, Lawrence won a purple district that used to belong to the Democrats’ patron saint of centrism, former CIA analyst Elissa Slotkin.

Even some of the defeats were surprisingly good for the left. In ruby-red Florida — where Republicans outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million and a Democrat hasn’t won statewide office since 2012 — DSA member Angie Nixon lost by less than three points, little different from the two-point losing margin of the ex-Republican candidate who Democrats ran for governor. The state’s last four Democratic losing margins for Senate are 13, 16, 0.2, and 8 points. And that’s after being outspent nearly four to one and getting no help whatsoever from the national Democratic Party, which should be kicking itself for missing the opportunity to win another gettable Senate seat.

That a DSA member would even be competitive in Florida — the heartland of right-wing Cuban extremism and the home of both Marco Rubio and now two Bolsonaro sons — would have sounded laughable five years ago, or even five months ago. That Nixon could do this well with this little help will, together with El-Sayed’s win, make it that much harder to argue that the socialist label is an inherent electoral liability.

It should spark some soul-searching among the Democratic establishment and its decision to preemptively write off the race as a foregone loss. But it will no doubt also spark debate within the socialist movement, too, given Nixon’s result was built partly on distancing herself from alienating positions like defunding the police and abolishing prisons. Her strong showing, along with the success of other left-wing candidates who similarly moderated or eschewed contemporary left orthodoxy on some issues, points to the benefits of DSA candidates having the flexibility to tailor campaigns to local electorates.

The US left also suffered a defeat of sorts in Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn fell short at a second tilt at a Senate seat in a state where a Democrat hasn’t won statewide election for 20 years. Osborn, a union leader who led a successful 2021 strike against Kellogg’s over planned benefit cuts, was something of a proof of concept for the left: that, as per 

research

 from the Center for Working-Class Politics, the way to win in such states is to run genuine working-class candidates with populist platforms outside of the Democratic Party brand.

To some extent, both of Osborn’s campaigns proved this true. The last four Democratic losing margins in Nebraska Senate races were 41 points, 19 points, 24 points, and 16 points; by contrast, Osborn has fallen short by roughly the same, single-digit margin of seven points both runs. Clearly, if pro-working-class candidates are going to flip a deep red state like Nebraska, Osborn’s campaign is a model for how to do it.

But a losing margin is still a loss. Despite combining left-populist policies like “right to repair” with centrist messaging on issues like immigration — Osborn famously ran ads declaring he backed Trump’s border wall — the former union leader was unable to shake attacks that he was a secret Democrat. A particularly damaging set of “

scandals

” had Osborn on tape bashing the border wall and other Trump policies and using insulting language about his voters. On top of an avalanche of 

outside spending

 aimed against him, it proved too much to overcome.

These are on top of a few other stinging defeats for the left, including Justice Democrats–backed Justin Pearson’s 

razor-thin loss

 in Tennessee’s Ninth District, who looked like he might be able to overcome a Republican gerrymander thanks to a surge in black voter turnout.

Socialists may instead be heartened by the 

victory

 of Scott Houldieson over a Trump-endorsed candidate in the Republican-held Indiana First Senate District. Houldieson, a union autoworker who cofounded and led the 

reform effort

 within the United Auto Workers that resulted in 

Shawn Fain’s

 leadership of the union, easily flipped the seat with a 14-point victory on the back of an affordability-focused campaign. Though not DSA-backed or a statewide race, it is to some extent a vindication of the kind of approach the left believed would see success in Nebraska.

Meanwhile, as usual, socialists and progressives continued their steady accrual of elected office at the state and local levels.

As of the time of writing, DSA has 

notched

 130 wins in everything from state legislatures and city councils to mayor’s offices and ballot measures, with 42 losses and 58 races still to be decided. While Angie Nixon fell short of her Senate bid, environmentalist Ashley Herrmann 

became

 only the second socialist to win elected office in Florida and the first to be elected to its state legislature in more than a century, flipping a swing district that the Republican incumbent had won with 

58 percent

 of the vote two years earlier. Other notable socialist wins included 

Robert LeVertis Bell’s

 election to the Kentucky state house and Mathewos Samson’s 

election

 to the Georgia General Assembly, which, together with Gabriel Sanchez’s reelection, makes him one of two socialists in the state legislature.

Particularly notable are several mayoral races that were foregone conclusions after the primaries. 

Janeese Lewis George

 is now officially Washington, DC’s first socialist mayor, having won on the back of an 

affordable housing

 plan that combines “abundance”-style reforms with expanding rent stabilization. In Providence, Rhode Island, socialist 

David Morales

 has similarly cruised to an expected win and, together with a socialist-led city council, will now work to pass a robust rent control measure in the housing-crisis-stricken city — a measure the incumbent mayor he successfully primaried had vetoed.

More complicated is the Los Angeles mayoral race, where socialist City Councilor Nithya Raman was on track to unseat Karen Bass at the time of writing as Los Angeles mayor. Raman’s candidacy was the subject of 

some controversy

, after she was endorsed by the local DSA chapter despite 

not fully embracing

 the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement against Israel and not being questioned about it, leading the DSA’s National Political Committee to nearly 

strip her

 of the endorsement, an effort that failed by one vote. If Raman does win, she’ll be the first candidate to unseat an incumbent LA mayor in 21 years.

This is on top of a host of progressive ballot measures pushed through by majorities of voters countrywide: the 

defeat

 of an abortion ban ballot measure in Missouri, a 

successful ban

 on dark money in elections in Montana, and divestment 

from Israel

 in Providence, to name a few. Maybe most notably, ballot measures restricting the construction of data centers have so far 

won overwhelmingly

 around the country, 38 to one, with eight still to be counted — a clear public vindication of a position championed and popularized by the broad left.

For the past decade, socialists and progressives have often had good election nights even when the Democratic Party has suffered, and they have had bad nights while Democrats rejoiced. The 2026 midterms may be the first election where both the left and the centrist party establishment have seen historic wins in tandem.

Over the past two years, the US left showed it was the force most willing to fight against Trump’s right-wing assault and to come up with an effective argument — affordability and fighting oligarchy — to do it. This election finally proved that left policies and rhetoric are not the electoral liability Democratic voters have been told for decades they are.

For decades, Democratic voters have had to make the agonizing decision every election to choose between their heads and their hearts. The left may have just freed them of it.

author: Fikayo Akeredolu
title: Nigeria's petrol subsidy was also an electricity policy
content:
As long as households and businesses in Nigeria depend on generators and cannot rely on the grid for electricity, some form of fossil fuel subsidy will always be necessary. Despite the costs, and despite what the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the climate research community say. This is because fossil fuel subsidies, in my opinion, are the country’s largest and most decentralized electricity access program, and any attempt at reform without explicitly accounting for this will fail. This essay explains why.

As a starting point, I need everyone to read Dr. Neil McCulloch’s book 

Ending Fossil Fuel Subsidies

. The book explains how subsidies are effectively a political prosthetic. Imagine you run a developing country with weak administrative capacity. You cannot reliably deliver schools or clinics, but you need to give citizens something that shows you are on their side and ensures you stay in power. Cheap energy through fossil fuel subsidies is the one thing you can deliver somewhat easily. Weak states, like Nigeria, lean on subsidies because a subsidy is a substitute for the public goods the state cannot otherwise provide.

author: Doha Ali
title: There are no apolitical girls in war
content:
“Doha, come sit with us. We need to talk to you.”

I was 15 years old, had just finished high school, and was getting ready to start university in Sudan. My mother knocked on my bedroom door and asked me to come into the living room. My parents were waiting for me.

“We need you to understand something important,” my father began. “When you go to university, don’t talk about politics.”

I remember asking the only question that made sense to me. “What is politics?”

My father paused for a moment before answering. “Politics is the art of what is possible,” he said. “It’s how people pursue what they believe can be achieved.”

I stared at him, trying to make sense of words that felt much too big for a 15-year-old. Before he could explain any further, my mother interrupted him.

“No,” she said quickly. “Politics is what old people talk about.”

She looked directly at me. “You shouldn’t talk about it. Bad things can happen if you do.”

That was the lesson I understood.

Politics was dangerous.

Looking back, I realize that my parents were not trying to teach me politics. They were trying to teach me how to survive.

The conversation was not unique to me. My older brother had already had it. So had my sister. When I arrived at university, I discovered that almost all of my friends had grown up with some version of the same warning.

author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
title: El Fasher, a year later
content:
Nasr City, October 26, 2026

Today is the anniversary, and I still don’t know what that word is supposed to do for anyone.

I was in Cairo when the city fell. I disappeared there — not in any way a person standing outside me could have seen — and I am not leaving that out, as if the one doing the remembering were a pane of glass. But El Fasher sits on an older arithmetic, and the arithmetic is where I have to start.

The old arithmetic

I was in the street in Omdurman on International Women’s Day in 2019, a month before they finally put Omar al-Bashir out of the palace he had occupied for 30 years. Three out of every four people in that crowd were women. The proportion mattered because NISS — the National Intelligence and Security Service, Sudan’s secret police, who have spent decades learning exactly where a society keeps its weight — knew where to look. They find it. Then they go after it.

So they started arresting the women.

There was nothing accidental in this, and nothing hidden. They were not ashamed, because shame requires believing someone is watching who matters, and they did not believe that. If the police took a man that day, it cost almost nothing to get him back: a friend, a cousin, anyone his age from his own street could walk into that station the same afternoon and walk him out again, because a man’s word, in that system, was still worth something on its own.

title: Tanzania’s peace was never peaceful
content:

author: Wini Omer
title: It’s not the refugees, it’s the austerity measures!
content:
A Sudanese journalist, with whom I worked for two years at the same newspaper, told me when I contacted him to check on his situation after the last wave of attacks against refugees in Libya: “We are trapped in our homes. We can’t leave. I didn’t send my kids to school since the beginning of this wave of violence. The situation is difficult beyond imagination.”

The Sudanese who left Sudan seeking refuge in Libya, amid very violent clashes that started in April 2023 and continue to this moment, are facing violence, danger, and hatred in what was supposed to be a safe refuge. But this reality is not exclusive to Sudanese refugees, and the violence is indifferent to other nationalities who are fleeing conflicts, war, and instability at home: Ethiopians, Eritreans, and refugees from the Central African Republic.

In Libya, African refugees faced waves of violence, the latest in June this year. Despite competing for power, Libya’s rival authorities in the east and west have united in stoking anti-migrant rhetoric and launching a violent campaign of mass detention and expulsions against migrants and refugees, as a recent 

Human Rights Watch report

title: Morocco’s long game
content:
“A bad system will beat a good person every time.” The words of Dr. Deming, a pioneer of systems thinking, perfectly encapsulate the problems faced by Moroccan football throughout the 2000s. 

At the turn of the century, on paper, it seemed like Moroccan football was in a pretty good place. In 1998, it was ranked 13th globally by FIFA. The team’s performance at the 1986 World Cup, when Morocco became the first African and Arab country to advance to the knockout rounds, was monumental.

Despite these early successes, Morocco would subsequently not qualify for a World Cup for the next 20 years. By 2014, Moroccan football would hit rock bottom, with FIFA ranking it 81st in the world — a precipitous decline. 

But as many of us know, by 2022 Morocco had risen to the top of international football. The team defeated major World Cup players, such as Portugal and Spain, becoming the first African and Arab country to advance to the semifinals.

author: Rachel Dubale
title: Eyes open in Addis
content:
If I squeeze my eyes shut and cover them with my hands, perhaps all of this will disappear. My father used to tell me something similar when, at an age perhaps already too old for it, I would whisper to him: “I’m afraid of the dark.”

“

Richo

,” he would say, “why in the world would you be scared of the dark? The dark is something we can make and unmake. See?” He would then cover my eyes with his big, calloused hands. “I made the dark for you.” And so I would fall asleep, covering my eyes with my hands and making my own dark.

So many years have passed since then — years in which I have learned not only how to make my own dark, but how to fill my eyes with the brightest colors: the green of my fields, the yellow suns of the Antilles, and the red of those tomato sauces shared over plates of pasta with the people I love.

With time I have also learned, and wanted 

more

author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
title: How a child inherits care
content:
We are sitting at Gallal. It’s in Madinaty, on the edge of Cairo where the buildings are all new and the streets are too wide. The tea is too sweet the way Sudanese tea is supposed to be too sweet when someone else makes it for you. Mahmoud is across from me.

I don’t remember either of us standing up. Only the hug itself, which went on long enough that an Egyptian girl at the next table put down her phone and started crying. She didn’t know us. She cried because whatever passed between two men holding on to each other in the middle of that cafe was apparently visible even to a stranger who had no context at all.

Mahmoud went red immediately — a Sudanese man has no idea what to do with a stranger’s tears — so he pulled out his phone, opened Facebook, and muttered that she was probably crying over some relationship, while the screen in his hand played footage of Khartoum burning. We’re good at that silence now. The silence of being physically tethered to one place while completely living inside another. I kept thinking: Does everyone I love do the same? Carry so much that they stop feeling it, until a stranger has to cry for them?

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Why does Tunisia become African only when Europe needs it to be?
content:
Tunisia is an African country that has spent much of its modern political imagination looking north. That sounds like a question of identity. In reality, it is a question of power — and more precisely, a practice of domination through classification.

For decades, Tunisia has imagined its economic future through the Mediterranean: European markets, French education, tourism, and European investment. Africa has often appeared somewhere beyond the Sahara, associated with instability, migration, and security.

Europe, however, possesses its own geography of Tunisia — one that shifts depending on what Europe needs from it. When Brussels discusses trade, investment, and political cooperation, Tunisia is a Mediterranean neighbor. When Europe discusses migration, border control, Libya, or the Sahel, Tunisia becomes something else: an African frontier state.

This is not a mere contradiction. This is a deliberate mechanism of geopolitical subordination through classification. Europe does not need Tunisia to be culturally European; it needs Tunisia to be strategically African when African space becomes relevant to European security.

The economic relationship makes this asymmetry impossible to ignore, revealing a genuine policy cage. The European Commission identifies the EU as Tunisia’s largest trading partner. In 2025, the EU accounted for 59.5% of Tunisia’s total trade. Some 73.2% of
